issues.title: Mostly Theoretical deadlock in Key Initation procedure
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
In the intial procedures we currently have these steps: 
`9. The server key manager receives Certificate/CertificateVerify/Finished,
   it exports the server key
   material for both the Primary and Restart DKCs, and installs it
   as its read (receive) key and as its write (send) key.

10. The server key manager calls Require Protected SCTP Packets to
    enforce DTLS chunk protection for all future packets and informs
    the ULP that the association is protected.

11. The server key manager sends a Protection Established control
    message ({{protection-established}}) to the client key manager.

12. The client key manager receives the Protection Established
    control message, exports all Primary and Restart DKC keys,
    and installs the server key material as its write (send) key,
    calls Require Protected SCTP Packets to enforce
    DTLS chunk protection for all future packets, and informs the
    ULP that the association is protected.`

In this procedure there exists a potential for deadlock that is uncertain if you even can make it trigger. But the case that exist here is the following:

When step 10 is completed the server only accepts protected packets. Then in step 11 it sends a encrypted Protection Established (PE) message to the client. At this point the client doesn't have a write key installed, only the read key. The server requires the client to send encrypted packets for them to reach the server and actually be processed. This situation lasts until the client receives the PE message, which triggers it to install the write key and also enable protection following step 12. 

So if the a SCTP packet carrying the PE message (or part of it) is lost between the server and the client, the client can't send any SACK that will actually reach the server. However, if the server does not receive the PE message its retransmission timer will fire and retransmit the non acked PE message. Thus, a true deadlock can only occur if the SCTP association at this stage would require a SACK message or some other control message to complete the transmission of the PE. 

So the question here is if this very unlikely situation needs to be addressed? 

One way of addressing this is to add additional control messages:
10. Server sends Protection Ready (Encrypted) -> Client
11. Client installs write key and sets Protection Required
12. Client sends Protection Established (Encrypted) -> Server
13. Server receives and sets Protection Required. Notifies ULP
14. Server sends Protection Established (Encrypted) -> Client
15. Client receives Protection Established, sets Protection Required and Notifies ULP

This procedure adds one RTT at minimal. Steps 14 and 15 is there to ensure that there are coordination of the ULP activation. It may be possible to skip 14 and 15 and instead have the client activate ULP at the end of step 12. But, that puts implementation requirements on server to prevent unprotected data to be delivered to ULP while delivering protected.

issues.title: Improving the initial handshake procedure
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
During the latest meeting with  @tuexen we discussed some aspect of the draft initial procedure and potential for improvements.

Two main insights came from that discussion.
- The current process kind of assumes that the KeyManager method do understand TLS messages, i.e. need to parse them to know where TLS is in the process to trigger the right steps.
- The current process is poorly addressing if an endpoint only want to be client, and thus should be sufficient to be only using a TLS client implementation, rather than having to have both server and client. 

Thus, some exploration of improvement of how the procedure works and how it interacts with the TLS session.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
In the meeting we did discuss also about the relevance for resumption of the TLS sessions. From Ericsson's perspective this is an optional feature that needs to be supported for the following performance reasons:
- Resumption results in that one don't send the whole certificate chain. This saves significant amount of message sizes, especially for the PQC certificates that is being rolled out that can be significantly bigger than any Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman (ECDH) based ones. 
- This also saves a bit on processing and thus energy and latency. 

Session resumption tickets can be pushed by the server at any point after the handshake has completed or they could explicitly be requested by the TLS client from the TLS server. Based on this it appears that we likely will need the TLS client to be the one initiating the TLS session closure to ensure that it has had the chance to send a ticket request and the server not having prematurely closed the TLS session before it can be responded to.

comments.author: teiclap
comments.body:
There's also the need to explain that the KM is the only Client of SSID 4242, thus it offers a transport service to TLS by encapsulating its messages, furthermore in section 7 we talk about PE message in a way that is not actual anymore.
I'm going to edit all this.

issues.title: Drain Timer and what is "last rekeying message"?
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
The Drain Timer Consideration section states: 

`If delivery of the last rekeying message has been confirmed (e.g., through SCTP acknowledgment of the DATA chunk carrying the TLS Finished)`

What is the "last rekeying message"? I think this can be improved now that we have updated the procedure to be clearer, and in fact I think we likely can consider to reduce the timer value even further than one MSS, as if one have received the RKI message this is solely the time an outstanding packet that has been reordered would be meaningful to arrive. Thus I think 3 seconds would be plenty of time.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: With the procedure we have the transmission of the RKI on the server side to the client starts the drain timer. At this point the client have's the key, just have not installed it's write key. If the servers drain time fires before the server's RKI reaches the client then the server will no longer be able to receive the client's packets. The server side will retransmitt the RKI using its retransmitt timer until the association fails. So I think the general structure is likely correct that the server should not set its drain timer to a low value until it has comfirmation that its RKI has been delivered. So I think a small update clarifying that this text discusses the RKI message. And likely the confirmed case can be reduced to a lower value of 3 or 5 seconds.

issues.title: Improved trigger of drainage after rekeying
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
The procedure in the drainage of the old epoch (Section 6.2.3) is problematic. The issue is really about that the server initiate the drainage in step 7: 

`The server key manager proceeds only after both its own TLS handshake has completed (7a) and it has received the client key manager's Read Key Installed control message (7b). Once both conditions are met, it exports both direction key material for both the Primary and Restart DKCs for epoch N+1, installs both the read (receive) key and the write (send) key, starts the drain timer to remove the old (epoch N) DKC, and switches sending to the epoch N+1 DKC. The server key manager sends a Read Key Installed control message (Section 4.2.1) to the client key manager.`

However, the client will not install its write key until it receives the RKI from the server. At this point no more SCTP packets using the old extension should be generated. If one knows this has happened then one can safely run a short timer (like 3 seconds) just to ensure that any delayed or reordered packets leaves the network. However, if you don't have an explicit indication of the delivery then the server can't really run a shorter timer than the failure to avoid impacting the ULP. If the RKI would be lost and delayed triggering the drain timer on the server side prior the client starting sending with the new epoch will impact the ULP. So the choice is between T_fail (303 seconds) and 3 seconds. Leaving a longer window of opprotunity for an attacker after a rekey. 

The main issue is that there are no ensured mechanism for the server to know that a particular message has been delivered unless one drain the whole association. Also this would mean an implementation requirement. 

Thus I think we should consider an additional KM message "Rekey Completed" sent by the client to the server, and use server reception of this to start the drainage timer. Thus avoiding all the issues.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: Discussed with @tuexen that easiest solution is to add an SCTP API notification when DTLS Chunk's API sees a new (higher) DTLS epoch. Notification of first use of a Read Key. @tuexen to propose PR for DTLS chunk. @gloinul to write PR to use it in handshake.

issues.title: When should the restart DKC be owerwritten during restart
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
Currently the restart section's step 7-12 says it is like Initial. However, this is actually not quite true. There is one important difference and why this may actually be better to model on the rekeying. Namely that the overwriting of the old restart DKC (especially for epoch 3 replacing epoch 3) needs to consider what to do with draining. If one overwrites Restart Epoch 3 directly after the primary write key is in place there will be no drain on the restart. And the spec allows ULPs to use the restart for its own traffic to ensure application session continuation. Thus, there is a point of draining the restart after the primary have been used. 

To make this procedure fast, I would recommend that we resolve issue #52 and in that solution ensures that the server can know when the client has put its write key in place and based on that can wait a short time and then overwrite the restart DKC in its association. 

This procedure may also need to consider when the persistent storage should be overwritten. That maybe should be overwritten as soon as the primary write key and the new restart DKC has been genereated but that requires more thought.

The prototype implementation is different, the rekey procedure is copied rather than the initial.
I agree that restart requires the old R-DKC to survive during the drain time, but rekey doesn't mention R-DKC: a possibility is to explain in the rekey sections that the rekey procedure is applied considering in this case R-DKC, on the other hand during rekey also R-DKC must be replaced at the same time as the normal DKC.
